questions.stem: A Developer Productivity agent built on the Claude Agent SDK is asked to investigate why a legacy billing module and an unrelated legacy shipping module both fail after a shared library upgrade. The team wants both investigations to run in parallel, and each subagent should know only what it needs about the shared library change, not the coordinator's entire prior exploration history. Which approach best achieves this?

options.text: Launch a single subagent and have it investigate both modules sequentially so context stays consistent.

Launch two Task invocations in the same response, each with an explicit prompt that states the relevant shared-library change and the specific module to investigate, without passing the coordinator's full transcript.
Launch the two subagents but let them inherit the coordinator's full conversation automatically so they don't miss any relevant detail.
Launch the two subagents in separate turns, one after another, so the coordinator can review the first result before deciding whether to start the second.

questions.stem: A team built a single Claude Agent SDK agent that both explores an unfamiliar codebase (reading files, tracing call graphs) and generates boilerplate code changes in the same context. As the codebase grows, the agent increasingly proposes changes based on stale or partial exploration because exploration output and generation reasoning compete for the same context budget. What is the most effective architectural fix?

options.text: Give the single agent a larger context window so it can hold both exploration output and generation reasoning at once.
Keep the single agent but add a stricter system prompt instructing it to "prioritize recent exploration over old exploration."
Split the work into a coordinator that delegates exploration to a specialized subagent and only passes the subagent's distilled findings to a separate step that performs code generation.
Alternate the single agent between exploration and generation more slowly, one file at a time, so it never explores too much before generating.

questions.stem: A developer productivity tool always runs the same fixed four-step pipeline for every incoming request: (1) full-repo Grep scan, (2) call-graph trace, (3) generate boilerplate, (4) write tests — regardless of whether the request is a one-line typo fix or a multi-file refactor. Users complain that trivial requests take as long as complex ones and burn unnecessary tokens. What should change?

options.text: Keep the fixed pipeline but run all four steps in parallel instead of sequentially to reduce wall-clock time.
Keep the fixed pipeline but increase the number of retries allowed per step so complex requests succeed more often.
Remove the call-graph trace step entirely from the pipeline since it is the most expensive step.
Replace the fixed sequential pipeline with dynamic task decomposition that assesses request complexity first and skips or scopes steps (e.g., no call-graph trace for a one-line fix) accordingly.

questions.stem: A developer's multi-hour Claude Code session investigating a legacy authentication system crashes two-thirds of the way through, after significant call-graph tracing and note-taking inside the conversation. The developer wants to continue without losing the investigation's key findings, but also doesn't want to replay every intermediate tool call from the crashed session. What is the best way to continue?

options.text: Start a new session and explicitly inject a written summary of the key findings from the crashed session, rather than replaying the stale raw tool call history.
Start a brand-new session and re-run the entire investigation from scratch to guarantee a clean, consistent context.
Resume the crashed session by name/ID so all raw tool outputs replay automatically, then manually skip past ones that are no longer needed.
Fork the crashed session at its very last turn so the new session inherits the identical state, including any now-stale tool results, and continue from there.

questions.stem: In a Developer Productivity agent, a request to 'find every caller of parseInvoice()' most often returns incomplete results because the agent tends to reach for Glob first. Separately, when the agent tries to edit a config value that appears identically in 30 places in one file, the Edit tool fails because it cannot find a unique anchor. What combination of fixes addresses both issues?

options.text: Use Glob for locating files by content pattern, and increase the Edit tool's retry count so it eventually succeeds on the ambiguous anchor.

Use Grep for the content search (finding callers by matching text across files) and, when Edit cannot resolve a unique anchor, fall back to a Read-then-Write of the full file with the disambiguated change.
Use Grep for both tasks, since it is the more powerful general-purpose tool for any content or path-based lookup.
Use Glob for the content search and ask the user to manually specify line numbers for the ambiguous Edit target.

questions.stem: A single Developer Productivity agent is equipped with 18 tools spanning file I/O, three different MCP code-search servers, a linter, a test runner, a deployment tool, and a Slack notifier, so that it can 'handle anything a developer might ask.' The team notices the agent frequently invokes the wrong tool among several with overlapping purposes (e.g., its own MCP search vs. built-in Grep) even for simple lookups. What is the most effective fix?

options.text: Keep all 18 tools available everywhere, but add a longer system prompt that lists, in prose, when to prefer each tool.
Keep all 18 tools, but switch to a larger model so it can reason more carefully about which tool to pick.
Scope each subagent or task context to a small, relevant subset of tools (roughly 4-5) instead of exposing all 18 tools everywhere, and remove or merge overlapping tools where possible.
Remove the deployment tool and Slack notifier since they are used least often, leaving the remaining 16 tools as-is.

questions.stem: A team adds a custom MCP code-search server intended to replace ad hoc use of the built-in Grep tool for a large monorepo, because the MCP server understands the project's module boundaries. The MCP tool does appear in the agent's available tool list for every session in this repo, so registration is not the issue. After integration, the agent keeps using built-in Grep instead of the new MCP tool for most searches. What is the most likely root cause and fix?

options.text: The MCP server is registered in `~/.claude.json` (personal) instead of `.mcp.json` (project-shared), so other tools aren't aware it exists.
Disable the built-in Grep tool entirely so the agent has no alternative but to use the MCP search tool.
Increase the MCP tool's timeout so it responds faster than Grep and gets selected more often.

The MCP tool's description is generic and doesn't clearly convey why or when it should be preferred over Grep; rewrite its description with concrete guidance and examples so the model's tool-choice reasoning favors it for module-aware searches.

questions.stem: A developer productivity tool is asked to convert a monolithic order-processing service into three separate microservices, touching shared data models, API contracts, and deployment config across many files. The team's default habit is to let Claude Code start editing directly, planning as it goes. What should change for this specific request?

options.text: Use plan mode first, since this is a large-scope, multi-approach architectural change where reviewing the proposed design before any file changes reduces costly rework.
Continue with direct execution, but ask Claude Code to work in smaller increments so any mistakes are easier to revert.
Continue with direct execution, since Claude Code will automatically switch into plan mode on its own if the change turns out to be complex.
Use plan mode, but only after direct execution has already produced a first draft, so the plan can be compared against real code.

questions.stem: Several developers on a team repeatedly ask Claude Code to generate a new REST endpoint following the same five-step boilerplate pattern (route, handler, validation schema, test stub, docs entry). The team wants this codified so any developer can trigger it consistently and reuse it across many unrelated repositories. Where should this be defined?

options.text: As a project-level CLAUDE.md section describing the five steps in prose, so it's loaded automatically every session in this repo.
As a reusable Skill (with SKILL.md front matter defining the procedure and allowed tools) that can be invoked on demand and shared or reused across repositories.
As a personal `~/.claude/commands/` slash command, since only the original author needs it.
As a `.claude/rules/` file scoped to the repo's `src/routes/**` glob, so it's automatically applied whenever those files change.

questions.stem: A developer asks Claude Code to 'modernize this legacy inventory module' with no further detail. Claude Code produces a large, confident rewrite in one pass, but it turns out to solve a different problem than the developer actually needed, wasting a full review cycle. For this kind of vague, high-stakes request, what change to the interaction pattern would most reduce wasted rework?

options.text: Have Claude Code generate three alternative rewrites in parallel so the developer can pick the best one after the fact.
Have Claude Code generate the rewrite as before, but attach a longer explanation of its reasoning so the developer can catch mistakes faster during review.
Have Claude Code ask a small number of clarifying questions first (an interview-style pattern) and confirm scope/expected input-output examples before generating the full rewrite.
Switch to a larger model so it is less likely to misinterpret the vague request.

questions.stem: A structured data extraction pipeline pulls invoice fields (vendor, amount, due_date, PO_number) from scanned PDFs into JSON using tool use with a JSON schema. For invoices where the PO_number is genuinely absent from the source document, the pipeline sometimes fabricates a plausible-looking PO number instead of leaving the field empty, even though the JSON always validates against the schema. What is the most effective fix?

options.text: Add a few-shot example showing a correctly filled PO_number so the model learns the expected format more precisely.
Add a stricter regex pattern to the PO_number field's schema so malformed values are rejected.
Switch to a larger model, since fabrication is a reasoning failure that a more capable model would avoid.
Make the PO_number field nullable in the schema (rather than required) so the model has a valid way to represent "not present" instead of inventing a value.

questions.stem: An extraction system trained mostly on one invoice template starts returning empty or badly mismatched fields for a new batch of documents from newly onboarded vendors whose layouts differ significantly (e.g., dates written as 'issued 3/4/26' instead of a labeled 'Due Date:' field). The prompt's field descriptions are already fairly detailed. What is the most effective next step to generalize to these varied formats?

options.text: Add 2-4 few-shot examples showing correct extraction from documents with clearly different layouts and phrasing, including one ambiguous case.
Rewrite the field descriptions to be even longer and more detailed in prose, without adding any example documents.
Lower the schema's validation strictness so more outputs pass without triggering errors.
Split the extraction into two separate calls, one for each vendor's template.

questions.stem: A contract-clause extraction system's instructions currently say 'flag any clause that seems risky, but only report the ones you're highly confident about.' Reviewers find this produces inconsistent flagging: similar clauses are sometimes flagged and sometimes not across different documents. What change would most improve consistency?

options.text: Keep the current instruction, but add 'be even more conservative' to reduce false positives further.

Replace the vague guidance with explicit, concrete criteria for what counts as a risky clause (e.g., named categories such as unlimited liability, auto-renewal without notice, unilateral termination), removing the subjective 'highly confident' framing.
Keep the current instruction, but ask the model to also report a self-reported confidence score alongside each flag so reviewers can filter by confidence.
Remove the flagging step's autonomy entirely and require the model to flag every clause so nothing is missed, leaving all filtering to human reviewers.

questions.stem: When an extraction call returns JSON that fails schema validation (e.g., 'amount' comes back as a string instead of a number), the current retry logic simply resends the same prompt with 'That was invalid, please try again.' This works about half the time and burns extra calls. Separately, some documents genuinely don't contain a required field at all, and retries never succeed for those. What is the best overall retry design?

options.text: Retry every failure the same generic way, but increase the maximum retry count from 3 to 10 so eventually one attempt succeeds.
Stop retrying altogether and route every validation failure straight to a human reviewer, regardless of whether it's a formatting issue or a genuinely missing field.

For schema/format validation failures, retry with a message that specifies exactly which field failed and why (e.g., 'amount must be a number, got a string'); for cases where the source document genuinely lacks the information, do not retry — treat it as a valid nullable absence instead.
For both failure types, switch the extraction call to a larger model so both formatting mistakes and missing-field cases resolve on the first attempt.

questions.stem: A team needs to run structured extraction over 50,000 historical contracts overnight to backfill a database; there is no user waiting for individual results and a same-day SLA is not required. Separately, a different part of the system performs extraction on a single newly uploaded document as part of an interactive user-facing upload flow that must respond within seconds. Which processing strategy fits each case?

options.text: Use the Message Batches API for both cases, since it is cheaper for any volume of extraction work.
Use direct synchronous calls for both cases, since Batch API cannot handle documents that require tool use or multi-turn correction.
Use the Message Batches API for the interactive upload (since batching reduces cost) and direct synchronous calls for the overnight backfill (since it will finish faster in aggregate).

Use the Message Batches API for the 50,000-document overnight backfill (cost-efficient, no strict latency requirement), and use direct synchronous API calls for the single-document interactive upload flow.

questions.stem: An extraction pipeline reports 97% field-level accuracy in aggregate, but the team wants higher confidence before shipping the output to a downstream finance system for a specific high-value field (total_amount). The same model instance that performed the original extraction is also asked to double-check its own output before finalizing. Reviewers later find several total_amount errors it did not catch. What change would most improve error-catching for this specific field?

options.text: Route total_amount through an independent second-pass instance that has no memory of the original extraction's reasoning, dedicated to verifying just that field, rather than relying on the same instance reviewing its own work.
Ask the same instance to re-read its own output one more time and confirm it looks correct before finalizing.
Trust the 97% aggregate accuracy figure and ship without additional verification, since it is already a high number.
Have the same instance produce three independent extractions of total_amount in the same conversation and take the majority value.

questions.stem: A structured extraction system reports 97% aggregate field accuracy across all document types and fields. A downstream team discovers that for one specific document type (handwritten receipts) and one specific field (tax_amount), accuracy is closer to 60%, but this is invisible in the aggregate number. What should the team change about how they measure and route for review?

options.text: Continue tracking only the aggregate accuracy number, since 97% is well above the team's general quality bar.

Break down accuracy by document type and field (not just in aggregate), and route low-performing type/field combinations (like handwritten receipts + tax_amount) through stratified human review rather than the same spot-check rate as everything else.
Raise the overall spot-check sampling rate uniformly across all documents so more errors are caught eventually, without changing which document types are sampled.
Remove handwritten receipts from the pipeline entirely, since they are dragging down the aggregate accuracy number.

questions.stem: An extraction system consolidates financial figures from three different quarterly source documents (an earnings report, a press release, and a regulatory filing) into a single output record. For one metric, the earnings report and the regulatory filing disagree by a large margin. The current implementation silently picks one value, without noting where it came from, and passes it downstream as the single "true" figure. What is the most defensible fix?

options.text: Keep picking one value automatically, but always prefer whichever source document was extracted first in processing order.
Average the two conflicting values so downstream systems get a single reasonable number.
Preserve a claim-to-source mapping in the output — retain both conflicting values, tag each with its source document, and surface the discrepancy rather than silently resolving it to one number.
Drop the metric entirely from the output whenever any two sources disagree, to avoid presenting a wrong number.

questions.stem: A structured extraction pipeline runs as several parallel subagents, one per document type. When the invoice-extraction subagent hits an unexpected encoding error and returns nothing for a batch of 200 documents, the coordinator logs this simply as 'processed 200 documents' since it received a response, and the downstream system silently receives 200 empty records. What is the correct way for the coordinator to handle this?

options.text: Treat any response from a subagent as successful processing, since the subagent did return without throwing an exception.
Retry the entire multi-type batch job (all document types, not just invoices) from the beginning whenever any single subagent has any issue.
Have the coordinator ignore subagent-level errors entirely and rely on the downstream finance system to catch any missing records after the fact.

Require subagents to return a structured error (e.g., distinguishing a genuine access/processing failure from a legitimate empty result) so the coordinator can detect the failure and retry, escalate, or flag those 200 documents rather than silently forwarding empty records.

questions.stem: During structured extraction from ambiguous legal documents, the pipeline occasionally hits clauses where two contradictory interpretations are both textually plausible and no schema rule resolves which is correct. The current design has the model pick one interpretation on its own and report a self-generated confidence score, escalating to a human only when its own confidence dips below 70%. Reviewers find several genuinely ambiguous clauses where the model reported 85%+ confidence but picked the wrong interpretation. What should change about the escalation trigger?

options.text: Base escalation on structural signals that indicate genuine ambiguity (e.g., detecting that a clause matches more than one mutually exclusive extraction pattern, or that required disambiguating context is missing) rather than relying on the model's self-reported confidence score, which is not a reliable proxy for correctness.
Increase the self-reported confidence threshold for escalation from 70% to 90%, so more borderline cases get escalated.
Remove escalation entirely and have a human review every single clause in every document, regardless of ambiguity.
Keep the self-reported confidence mechanism, but average it with a second independent instance's self-reported confidence before deciding whether to escalate.
